articles.title_orig: Barber says he had 'no choice' but to tackle driver who struck Australian MP Helen Haines
articles.title_zh: Barber says he had 'no choice' but to tackle driver who struck Australian MP Helen Haines
articles.content_orig:
Australian MP Helen Haines remains in a critical condition after being hit by a car in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese calls "a deliberate act"
The suspect allegedly did a U-turn in order to strike the MP and then reversed to ram her a second time , Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke says
The 65-year-old independent MP, who was taken by helicopter to hospital in Melbourne, has reportedly lost a leg
A 43-year-old man, from nearby Tarrawingee, was detained at the scene by a passer-by before being taken into custody
Police say it was an 'isolated incident' and they are working to identify potential charges
Both MPs and experts have warned that threats to Australian politicians were rising before the Haines incident, writes Tiffanie Turnbull in Sydney
Edited by Helen Livingstone, with Katy Watson in Wangaratta and Lana Lam in Sydney
An outpouring of thoughts and well wishes, in the form of flowers, has built up in the street outside Helen Haines' MP office in Wangaratta this morning.
The tributes illustrate Haines' popularity among members of her electorate.
New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon says he spoke with Anthony Albanese in the aftermath of the alleged attack on Helen Haines, and passed on "thoughts and prayers from New Zealand".
Speaking to journalists this morning, Luxon described the incident as a âterrible set of circumstancesâ.
"The facts haven't still come out as to what the motivation has been or was, but you know, a concerning development in Australia for sure," he said.
New Zealand's foreign minister Winston Peters said in an X post that "New Zealand is shocked by the attack on Australian MP Helen Haines".
"Violence has absolutely no place in politics," he wrote.
Katy Watson Australia correspondent reporting from Wangaratta
At the Holy Trinity Anglican Cathedral here in Wangaratta, thereâs a vigil taking place - several hundred people whoâve come to pay their respects and light a candle for Helen Haines who remains in hospital.
âItâs just something that you wouldn't expect in our community,â says Austin Longfild.
âYou see it in other countries and it's just something that I didn't comprehend could happen here, and then it's just happened down the street.â
Heâs full of praise for Helen Haines:

âSeeing how she advocates for the community, she seems pretty authentic,â he says. â©
âWhether you vote for her or not, she seems to have the community actually at heart so thatâs all you can really ask for, for a politician that represents your community.â
Ricky Jefferies says a "lot of people got involved immediately"
Helen Haines, the independent federal MP for Indi, remains in a critical condition in hospital after she was hit by a car outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, Victoria, yesterday afternoon.
Stay with us as we bring you the latest updates.
A man flies the Australian flag outside the office of Helen Haines
Local media are reporting the name of the 43-year-old man arrested yesterday as Brendan Nugent.
It's understood Nugent, from nearby Tarrawingee, was an environmental campaigner with an interest in anti-logging issues.
Nugent was detained by bystanders in the moments after he allegedly drove into Helen Haines outside her electorate office on Monday afternoon.
Haines remains in critical condition in a Melbourne hospital.
Katy Watson Australia correspondent reporting from Wangaratta
Helen Hainesâ office is on Wangarattaâs main street, which has now reopened to traffic and cars are slowly filing past.
On the window is a large decal of Dr Haines, smiling at her electorate.
This apparent attack has shocked this small community, and of course the country more broadly.
On the pavement outside her office, thereâs a growing number of bouquets being left for her.
Every so often, another member of the community walks by, stops, and lays another one down.
One card reads "may you recover quickly and continue to be a light in this world". Another thanks her for all the "wonderful" work she has done.
We know Helen Haines was taken to hospital with severe injuries to her lower body yesterday, and that she underwent surgery overnight after being airlifted to a Melbourne hospital.
This morning the Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported that the MP has lost one of her legs.
Nine News has also reported this.
The last we've heard from officials is that Haines is in a critical condition.
Fellow
independent MP Allegra Spender has been telling ABC News "many people have feared that there would be some
sort of violent incident against Australian politicians".
"I think this is of
huge concern, because I think we take pride in the fact that in Australia, politicians are just like anybody else, you treat them just like anybody else,
but theyâve got to be accessible, and thatâs really important," she says.
Asked if Australia
has been so far been sheltered from the type of political violence seen towards MPs in the UK, she says âweâve done better in this country, and we have to continue
to do better, and that means in terms of violence against politicians but
frankly - abuse of people in our hospitals, in our supermarkets."
"This is part
of a trend that we I think a country, not just as politicians, we need to step
up and say, we donât want to see this sort of violence in language and
violence in attitude."
"We are collectively responsible for that."
Political leaders have condemned the apparent attack on independent MP Helen Haines who remains in a critical condition in hospital.
Australia's opposition leader Angus Taylor says it is a "shocking day for our nation" and that Australians will be "angry and appalled" by the attack.
"Our nation cannot become a place where violent attacks are normalised," he says.
The Greens leader David Shoebridge says the notion that Haines was targeted for her work is "horrifying, senseless, and shameful".
âWe cannot let political violence become the norm and I believe that politics grounded in non-violence is a powerful way to address this threat.
And Senator Pauline Hanson , leader of One Nation, says: "Violence against any elected representative, whoever they are and whatever they stand for, is never acceptable in Australia".
Steve Manning, the independent candidate for Ovens Valley, in north-east Victoria, says that a vigil will be held for Helen Haines in Wangaratta this afternoon.
Manning told Australia's national broadcaster, the ABC, that those who wished to take part should come to the Holy Trinity Anglican Cathedral at 1pm local time.
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) Commissioner has just released a statement about Helen Haines with an update on the 43-year-old man who was arrested shortly after the incident.
The AFP and Victoria Police are "working closely together to identify potential charges," says Krissy Barrett, with possible state and Commonwealth offences including causing harm to a public official which carries a maximum penalty of ten years in prison.
"At this stage it appears this is an isolated incident, and there are no known threats connected to this matter," she says.
The investigation is being led by Victoria Police's security investigation unit with support from the state's joint counter terrorism team, which is includes the AFP and ASIO, Australia's spy agency.
Federal police have regularly raised concerns about "growing threats against federal parliamentarians and high office holders," Barrett says, and last October, a special unit was established to probe politically-motivated violence and hate, with 41 people charged as a result.
The head of Australia's intelligence services, Mike Burgess, has issued a statement warning that increased levels of "grievance, intolerance and polarisation continue to create a permissive environment of violence" in Australia.
He says that the agency, ASIO, is concerned about the "use of violent rhetoric in public discourse".

articles.title_orig: China’s new 0.1-nanometre electron microscope ready to challenge US and Japan
articles.title_zh: China’s new 0.1-nanometre electron microscope ready to challenge US and Japan
articles.content_orig:
Model marks shift from R&D to commercialisation and aligns with country’s effort to cut reliance on imported tech
China is ready to commercialise a 200-kilovolt transmission electron microscope with an information resolution down to 0.1 nanometres that could introduce a new challenger into a market long dominated by the US and Japan.
Developed by Hefei-based manufacturer CIQTEK, the microscope features a point resolution of 0.25nm and an information limit of 0.1nm – on par with leading workhorse models on the market.
This marks a shift for the country’s expanding advanced electron microscopy industry from research and development to commercialisation, according to a report by the official ministry newspaper Science and Technology Daily on Monday.
It also represents the latest achievement aimed at reducing the country’s reliance on imports of the technology used in vital advanced industries like chip manufacturing.

articles.title_orig: 'It smells like charred earth': BBC at Indonesia fire epicentre causing Singapore and Malaysia haze crisis
articles.title_zh: 'It smells like charred earth': BBC at Indonesia fire epicentre causing Singapore and Malaysia haze crisis
articles.content_orig:
The BBC is on the ground in Indonesia's Central Kalimantan where burning peatlands continue to blanket large parts of South East Asia in toxic smog
A pungent charred earth smell wafts through the air and smoke billows from the ground, as peatlands continue to burn underground, our Indonesia correspondent Liza Tambunan reports
The haze has brought toxic air to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and parts of the Philippines for weeks now. In Indonesia alone, tens of thousands have fallen ill
Pressure is mounting on Indonesia to stop the fires that are causing the haze, which have been made worse by an unusually strong El NiÃ±o
Singapore has warned companies blamed for the haze , saying its "determination to act" should not be underestimated
Edited by Joel Guinto, with Liza Tambunan and Haryo Wirawan in Central Kalimantan and Osmond Chia and Koh Ewe in Singapore
Public anger is simmering in Malaysia, where residents have spent weeks enduring toxic haze drifting from Indonesia's wildfires.
On the worst days, schools were closed for several days and popular tourist sites were obscured by a blanket of smog.
All this has given rise to a wave of anger among Malaysians, who are airing their frustrations about the yearly occurrence on social media.
Some lawmakers have also spoken out, saying Indonesia needs to be treated "as an outcast in the region" and questioning why Malaysians should be impacted by "irresponsible actions beyond our borders".
But the official response has been noticeably more subdued - as authorities  navigate the ticklish topic with its neighbour and longtime ally.
Malaysian President Anwar Ibrahim said last week that the government had "done everything we can" to engage Indonesia on the issue. Malaysia has offered to help Indonesia tackle its wildfires - though Indonesia has not taken it up.
For now, Malaysia says it would broach the issue through diplomatic channels, without threatening bilateral ties with Indonesia. The haze crisis is set to be discussed at a meeting of South East Asian ministers next month.
Adan Reporting from Palangka Raya
As thick haze from forest and land fires continues to choke Palangka Raya, one of the worst-hit cities in Central Kalimantan, residents have been seeking refuge inside "clean air shelters" set up by local volunteers.
The RAKAT coalition, a network of civil society groups, has been running two such shelters since August, offering facilities including air purifiers, oxygen, nebulisers and basic medicines. The shelters are open daily in the evenings.
Coordinator Agung Sesa said the initiative was launched to support residents affected by the worsening haze, particularly vulnerable groups such as children and older people.
The shelters receive around 10 to 15 visitors a day, many seeking help for breathing difficulties, persistent coughs and eye irritation.
"Most complaints involve shortness of breath, coughing and sore eyes," Agung said, adding that some visitors have required urgent treatment for respiratory conditions. Volunteers are seeking donations of medicines, vitamins, milk and oxygen supplies.
This morning our team observed residents in Palangkaraya, the capital of Central Kalimantan, going about their daily activities. This despite visible haze and the air quality sitting at "very unhealthy" levels, according to monitoring site IQAir.
Singapore has issued legal notices to 10 companies over the fires in Indonesia that it believes have contributed to haze in the region.
The firms are being ordered to halt burning on their land in Indonesia and furnish Singapore with their plans to put out the fires.
Investigations show that some of the recent haze come from fires on land owned by these firms in Indonesia, Singapore's National Environment Agency said.
Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said in a statement on Monday that his government will "pursue all available legal and regulatory avenues" to hold those responsible for the fires to account.
Authorities in the region are facing growing pressure to tackle the haze, but some observers warn that these measures could carry diplomatic risks.
Singapore issued a sharp warning to companies blamed for the haze, calling on them to stop burning and take action to contain the fires.
Senior Minister K Shanmugam told the media on Monday that Singapore is prepared to use "every legal and regulatory lever at our disposal" to pursue the firms responsible.
"They may think that it is hard to get evidence, and that they may think that they can escape scrutiny. But they should not underestimate the Singapore government's determination to act," said Shanmugam, who oversees the national security matters.
The island-state issued has issued legal notices to 10 firms linked to the fires, ordering them to halt burning on their land in Indonesia and to put out the flames.
Liza Tambunan Reporting from Palangka Raya, Central Kalimantan
I am currently in Palangka Raya, one of the areas worst affected by the forest and land fires that have been burning across Indonesia.
When I looked out the window this morning, I saw a thick haze blanketing the city. Visibility is limited. I cannot see very far out into the distance. Trees across the road are shrouded in smog.
The smoke is so thick I can look at the sun and see a small yellow, dimly lit circular object in the sky - almost like looking at a light fixture on the ceiling of my hotel room.
As I stepped outside onto the balcony, the stench of burnt earth immediately hit my nostrils. It felt like it was burning.
This is the reality that people have been living with here in Palangka Raya and its surrounding areas. Some have no choice but to continue to go on with their lives without an adequate mask, putting their health at risk with every breath they take.
Health officials Iâve spoken to here say thereâs been approximately a 25% spike in respiratory cases in recent months attributed to the fires and haze.
Osmond Chia Business reporter
The Kuala Lumpur skyline shrouded in haze
Jakarta has come under growing international pressure to do more to tackle the fires and the industry around it, straining ties in the region.
Earlier this month, the head of Indonesia's Government Communications Agency Syahganda Nainggolan defended his country, saying: "We're not just sending over the haze."
"When there's no haze, we send oxygen. The oxygen from Singapore and Malaysia is from our forests, right?" Nainggolan said.
Singapore Senior Minister K Shanmugam on Monday said the remarks were disappointing and that the comments were "not right" when people in the region are suffering from the haze.
He added that he believed the view was not shared by others in the Indonesian government and welcomed President Prabowo Subianto's efforts to tackle the crisis.
While Singapore has issued legal notices to firms linked to the the burning behind the haze, Malaysia has downplayed the need for such an approach, opting for diplomatic channels to address the issue for now.
Indonesia has not yet accepted offers of help from Singapore and Malaysia.
Liza Tambunan Reporting from Palangka Raya, Central Kalimantan
The continuous burning of peatland causes toxic haze to billow from the ground
In the car, our driver Yusron tells me he hasnât encountered prolonged haze like this before.
The 57-year-old Banjarmasin resident recalled devastating fires in 1997 and 2015, noting it was the monsoon rains that finally extinguished the flames back then.
"Weâre just waiting for the rainy season to put an end to this, but this year it seems to have been delayed," Yusron said.
Relief may be delayed, as Indonesiaâs weather agency reported a shorter rainy season starting in November, a month later than forecast.
Back on the road, the haze worsens as we approach Palangka Raya, thickening and glowing with a light yellow tint. Visibility is limited, forcing Yusron to slow down.

articles.title_orig: China warns UK against EU-style tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles
articles.title_zh: China warns UK against EU-style tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles
articles.content_orig:
Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package
No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.
Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme .
The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.
The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.
The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”. “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.
This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.
However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.
Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.
They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”
Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.
EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.
But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.
Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.
According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.
This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.
Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.
Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.
China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.
While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.
Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.
At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.
Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.
“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Asian shares tumble, oil rises as markets await AI sector results
articles.title_zh: Asian shares tumble, oil rises as markets await AI sector results
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Caroline Valetkevitch and Danilo Masoni
NEW YORK/MILAN, Oct 19 (Reuters) - The Nasdaq rose more than 1% on Monday as tech shares rebounded ahead of a big week for AI-related earnings, while European stocks and the euro fell as unrest in France added to concerns about the country's fiscal outlook.
French bonds and Paris-listed ‌stocks also fell as the widespread protests across France underscored the difficulties the government faces in reducing its large deficit.
France's central government asked some local authorities to ‌impose curfews as it faced pressure over security failings on Monday, after looting stemming from the protests.
Tech stocks on Wall Street recovered some ground after a bruising week, with an index of semiconductors up 1.6%. On Friday, the index ​sank in its eighth straight day of declines, its longest losing streak since 2008.
With results due from Meta on Wednesday, and results from Tesla and chipmakers Lam Research and Texas Instruments also due this week, investors will be watching for signs that massive AI spending ultimately pays off.
"Investors are buying the correction dip that we had," said Peter Cardillo, chief market economist at Spartan Capital Securities in New York.
"The market is now going to go through a very critical test over the next two weeks. We have some big-name earnings coming out," he said. "In terms of technology, the test ‌of whether or not the spending on AI... will be met ⁠with satisfaction is going to be critical."
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 36.38 points, or 0.07%, to 51,966.03, the S&P 500 rose 31.29 points, or 0.41%, to 7,690.73 and the Nasdaq Composite rose 290.85 points, or 1.11%, to 26,430.89. MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe rose 0.88 points, ⁠or 0.08%, to 1,129.98.
Meta is one of five AI hyperscalers expected to increase combined capital expenditure to about $1.2 trillion next year, according to Goldman Sachs.
Results from SpaceX are also due on Tuesday. Overall, US earnings are still expected to rise about 30%, largely driven by growth in the technology sector.
US Treasury yields rose on Monday, with the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield coming off its biggest weekly drop in seven ​months, ​as concerns about the impact of higher interest rates on AI stocks abated. The yield on the benchmark ​US 10-year Treasury note was up 4.2 basis points at 5.14%.
The recent ‌bond selloff had also intensified scrutiny of the AI sector's massive funding needs.
In economic data, the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market index on Monday showed a drop of three points to 29 this month, the lowest level since June 2012 and below the 31 estimate of economists polled by Reuters.
Recent comments from Federal Reserve officials, including Chair Kevin Warsh, suggest policymakers are in no rush to hike rates again. On Friday, Warsh expressed optimism about US economic strength but gave no indication of whether or when more hikes will be needed.
EUROPEAN STOCKS, EURO FALL
The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 0.8%, while France's blue-chip CAC 40 index dropped 1.1%.
France's 10-year yield earlier was up 13 basis points to 4.9% while the German 10-year yield, the ‌benchmark for the euro zone, was also higher. The spread between French OATs and safe-haven German Bunds ​has widened to 147 basis points, trading at levels last seen during the 2011 to 2012 European debt crisis, ​from around 110 bps in late September.
Widespread weekend unrest in the euro zone's second-largest ​economy underscored the challenge facing the French government as it seeks to reduce its large budget deficit ahead of next year's presidential elections.
The euro ‌fell 0.24% to $1.1212.
The US dollar was boosted by the rebound in tech ​stocks. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against ​a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, rose 0.17% to 101.97.
Meanwhile, the Australian dollar rose 0.49% versus the greenback after data showed China's economic growth rebounded from three-year lows, expanding at a 4.5% annual pace in the third quarter.
Oil prices were mixed, with investors digesting attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on a Yemeni military training ​camp and renewed attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military facilities.
Brent ‌crude futures fell 31 cents to settle at $109.55 a barrel. Brent fell more than $3 earlier in the session.
US West Texas Intermediate gained $2.25 to $103.66 a barrel, the highest ​settlement since September 15.
Spot gold fell 0.61% to $4,139.67 an ounce.
(Reporting by Caroline Valetkevitch in New York and Danilo Masoni in Milan; additional reporting by Wayne Cole ​and Avinash P; Editing by Stephen Coates, Kevin Buckland, Xevi Fontdegloria, Nick Zieminski and Deepa Babington)

articles.title_orig: Chinese AI idol’s ‘pregnancy’ stunt sparks backlash, debate over digital boundaries
articles.title_zh: Chinese AI idol’s ‘pregnancy’ stunt sparks backlash, debate over digital boundaries
articles.content_orig:
An observer notes that the moment it goes live, it commodifies a sensitive topic that should never be exploited
A Chinese AI girl group has sparked intense online backlash after announcing that one of its virtual members was “pregnant” to explain her departure.
BABYQUEEN, a four-member, K-pop-style AI girl group managed in Liaoning province in northeastern China, formed in September and has around 1,100 followers.
On October 13, the group posted an announcement written from member Mity’s perspective. Saying she was “pregnant” and would pause all public activities, Mity asked fans to respect her privacy and her new life, without identifying the “father.”
The post went viral, attracting more than 78 million views on Weibo and igniting fierce debate over the boundaries of humanlike identities for digital personas.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Russian diplomat condemns U.S.-Israel attacks in Tehran visit as Netanyahu tells Trump "we have a job to finish"
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Russian diplomat condemns U.S.-Israel attacks in Tehran visit as Netanyahu tells Trump "we have a job to finish"
articles.content_orig:
Iran's top security official called for stronger cooperation with Russia to bolster regional security after meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Tehran on Monday, Iran's state-run IRNA news agency said.
Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said that cooperation could include joint economic projects, such as the completion of transportation corridors. Lavrov, meanwhile, condemned the U.S.-Israeli military attacks on Iran as illegal during his first visit to Iran since the U.S. launched its war with Iran almost eight months ago.
Also in Tehran on Monday, Iran summoned Germany's ambassador over what it called baseless accusations, the Iranian Foreign Ministry said. Germany had summoned Iran's ambassador in Berlin the same day after a court sentenced two men with ties to Iran's intelligence service for plotting to kill the leader of a Jewish organization in Germany.
President Masoud Pezeshkian also said Iran is willing to resolve tensions through dialogue, blaming U.S. interference for divisions in the region, state-run IRNA reported.
Pezeshkian made the remarks during Monday's meeting with Lavrov, saying the presence of U.S. military bases in neighboring countries had only increased tensions, instability and insecurity.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu released a video on Monday of a phone call between him and President Trump, in which the two leaders traded praises and suggested they may again attack Iran together.
Netanyahu shared the call one day after Mr. Trump endorsed his reelection bid. In it, the U.S. president could be heard telling the prime minister on speakerphone: "I think you're going to have a tremendous victory, actually."
"You're the man I want by my side, Bibi," Mr. Trump said, referring to Netanyahu by his nickname.
בשיחה עם ידידי הנשיא טראמפ לאחר שהודיע על תמיכתו בי בבחירות. יחד אנחנו הולכים להסיר את האיום האיראני לתמיד! צאו להצביע מחל! pic.twitter.com/GuPEAPn0Tc
Netanyahu hailed Mr. Trump for joining Israel in attacking Iran in late February.
"Donald, we have a job to finish," a beaming Netanyahu said. "We'll finish it together. We'll finish it, and no one else will do it."
Netanyahu did not elaborate but again described Iran's clerical state, which remains in power nearly eight months after the joint attack, as "the greatest danger."
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement Monday that the group had carried out six military operations in Saudi Arabia over the previous 48 hours, amid a sharp escalation in hostilities between the Iran-backed group and the kingdom.
Saree said the attacks targeted military sites, airports and oil infrastructure, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Aramco facilities in Yanbu on the Red Sea coast, and the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates.
Other strikes hit Abha International Airport, radar installations, Khamis Mushait air base in southwestern Saudi Arabia, a Saudi naval force camp, and a separate radar site in Bir Askar in the kingdom's south, according to Saree.
He described the attacks as retaliation for more than 200 Saudi strikes and missile attacks on Houthi-held areas over the previous 48 hours, saying the Houthis would pursue a policy of "escalation for escalation" until attacks on Yemen cease.
On Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry blamed Saudi-led forces for airstrikes that killed or wounded more than 30 people in Yemen's rebel-held territory over the weekend, including one in the northern province of Saada that left at least nine dead. Five children and two women were among those killed, according to the rebel group.
At least 53 soldiers were killed and another 200 recruits were injured at a military camp on Monday, when Houthi rebels struck Yemeni forces with ballistic missiles, Yemeni military officials said. The targeted camp is in the southern province of Shabwa. The provincial government there also acknowledged the strike, as did the Iran-backed rebel group.
The attack was one of the deadliest since fighting resurged between the Houthis and Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces this summer, as a widening front in the Iran war that began in February.
The provincial government in Shabwa said the death toll from Monday's attack could rise.
"This bloody, treacherous attack targeted new recruits in the training and preparation phase and is considered an extremely critical military escalation and a blatant aggression on the security and stability of Shabwa province," the provincial government said in a statement, which also called on Yemen's president, the Saudi-led coalition and the government to expedite air defense and early warning systems to reinforce Shabwa's capabilities.
The head of Yemen's ruling Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, promised a "firm response" and said the attack reflects the Houthis' "approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter."
One Yemeni military official said the missiles struck while recruits were lining up in formation for a training session. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the media.
Residents of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital city, received alert messages from authorities on Monday that warned of "a hostile aerial threat." AFP journalists received the alerts, too, which were sent to their phones, according to the outlet.
"A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Riyadh City to alert of a potential danger," Saudi Arabia's civil defense agency said in a statement on X. The agency also reported that the same warning had been issued for the nearby Kharj area.
A woman in her thirties living in northern Riyadh said she heard the sound of explosions, telling AFP: "we got used to this."
The warning, which often signals incoming Houthi attacks, was lifted shortly after the defense agency's announcement. But it came as attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have intensified in Saudi Arabia. Hours later, the Houthis claimed a series of missile and drone attacks on Riyadh's international airport and other targets across the kingdom over the past two days.
A major Saudi investment conference has been postponed to next year, its chief executive officer said on Monday, as the kingdom comes under repeated attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
Maha Al Saud, the CEO of the annual Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute, said the event, which was scheduled to take place in Riyadh from Oct. 26 to 29, would instead happen in 2027 in a statement posted on X . She said organizers wanted to ensure the gathering's tenth anniversary edition delivered the "full scale" and "extraordinary quality" participants expected.
"This decision comes from a deep commitment to our partners, members, speakers and delegates," her statement said, adding: "A decade of partnership and shared vision deserves nothing less than our absolute best."
New conference dates will be announced soon, while current registrations and partnerships will remain valid, according to the statement.
For nearly a decade, the conference has served as a showcase for Saudi Arabia's efforts to attract global investors, business leaders and heads of state. The postponement dealt a blow to the kingdom's ambitions to draw foreign capital, diversify its oil-reliant economy and push its reform agenda.
Three sources familiar with the matter had earlier told AFP the conference would be postponed.
Egypt's parliament on Monday postponed its debate on President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's request to authorize military support to Saudi Arabia, which has faced mounting attacks from Yemen's Houthis, Egyptian state media reported. The debate has been delayed until next week, according to the report.

articles.title_orig: Hegseth makes unannounced trip and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Hegseth makes unannounced trip and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an undisclosed visit to Israel, according to Axios.
The meeting between the hawkish ally of US President Donald Trump and the veteran Israeli premier facing a knife-edge election occurred on Monday, Axios reported, citing two sources with knowledge of the matter.
The Reuters news agency could not immediately confirm the visit. The Pentagon and Israel’s embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and there was no immediate indication of what they discussed.
President Trump took to his social media platform Truth Social on Sunday to endorse Netanyahu in next week’s parliamentary election, the first vote since the Hamas-led October 7 attacks in 2023 and Israel’s genocidal campaign in Gaza began.
Trump praised the prime minister for being an ally of the US in its war on Iran. He added that Netanyahu had his “Complete and Total Endorsement”.
“BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” Trump wrote.
Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls suggest.
US Vice President JD Vance, however, declined to endorse Netanyahu in an interview earlier on Monday, saying he was not getting involved in Israeli elections.
“I endorse American candidates, and that’s where I’m focused on is the midterms,” Vance, who travelled to Budapest and endorsed Viktor Orban in Hungarian elections earlier this year, said in an interview with digital media outlet 2WAY.
“I’m not anti-endorsing him, but I’m not pro-endorsing him; I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections,” Vance said.

articles.title_orig: 'Our worst nightmare': Threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
articles.title_zh: 'Our worst nightmare': Threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
articles.content_orig:
Watch: Police give update after Australian MP hit by car
As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did.
Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory.
But MPs and public figures â backed by experts â have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter.
And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised.
Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta.
Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack.
He was briefed by federal police â whose counter-terror squad is helping state officers investigate â and told the national broadcaster: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."
Witnesses saw the suspect do a U-turn before striking the MP and then reversing to ram her again, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has said.
Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese has been emotional when he has spoken about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets.
The alleged attack has left Australia reeling
Earlier this year Albanese himself was evacuated from his official residence over a bomb threat. As of August, about 20 cases in which people were accused of making violent threats against him were winding their way through courts around the country.
In recent years, politicians here have been mailed bullets. Female MPs â and in some cases their children â have been threatened with sexual violence. A Jewish MP's office has been firebombed, a Sydney mayor's car has been torched and countless other politicians have had their workplaces vandalised.
Just last week Small Business Minister Anne Aly said she had received a wave of death threats after a politician from the opposition said she should be "shamed and stoned in the square" over a tax policy.
According to government statistics, there were 1,067 reports of "harassing and threatening behaviour" against "high office holders" in the year to June: an increase on last year.
"We tend to bury our head in the sand and say, 'Not here', but this has been happening now for well over a decade," Josh Roose, a Deakin University Professor on violent extremism, tells the BBC.
Socioeconomic strain, growing mental health problems in the community, "grifters" who benefit politically or financially from whipping up further discontent, and a "carcinogenic" online environment are drivers of the trend, he says, which has dramatically escalated since the pandemic.
But the political class must also take responsibility for their role, he adds.
"We've seen a willingness to cross previously sacred terrain - you know, not targeting individuals, not targeting their families - but we now see that this is part and parcel of Australian political life.
"This is occurring at both ends of the political spectrum."
And experts like him warn it is not just politicians who are vulnerable: it is members of the media, academics, court officials and other public figures too.
Australian MP critically injured after being hit by car in apparent attack
What we know about apparent attack on Australian MP hit by car
Mike Burgess, the head of Australia's domestic spy agency Asio, has warned for years that the spectre of political violence is looming in Australia.
"Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack," he said in his annual threat assessment for 2026.
And the federal police have said it is not just ideology motivating cases in recent times. "Grievance" is radicalising people.
"They're feeling distanced, they're feeling alone, they're looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose," Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC earlier this month.
Helen Haines at Parliament House in Canberra
In the wake of the attack, a range of MPs have described wearing disguises in public, locking their office doors, and scanning every crowd for potential threats.
Women in politics are particularly scared, said Victorian state MP Georgie Purcell, who shares part of her electorate with Haines.
"Being a woman in politics changes the way you move through the world. We consider where we park our cars, the route we drive home, if we hold public events," she said in a statement.
"For many of us, the news... is our worst nightmare".
Coalition Senator James Paterson told News24: "I'd like to say that I was surprisedâ¦ but I'm not at all surprised."
There have been frustrated rumblings in Canberra from some MPs who say security arrangements have not changed with the climate and â if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed â one of the greatest tenets of the nation's political culture could now be at risk.
It is not abnormal for you to run into your local member at the shops, or chat to them at the footy, and many open up their offices for constituents who want to raise concerns or share ideas.
Haines is particularly renowned and respected for that, Albanese said on Monday night.
"Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people," he said.
"I don't want to see a political system in which you can't have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums â that's an important part of our democracy."

articles.title_orig: Kim Jong Un ‘proof of life’ photos released by North Korea after wild rumors dictator died from brain hemorrhage
articles.title_zh: Kim Jong Un ‘proof of life’ photos released by North Korea after wild rumors dictator died from brain hemorrhage
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has released a fresh batch of apparent “proof of life” photos showing Kim Jong Un inspecting shoes and women’s clothing — after wild rumors swept social media claiming the dictator had died from a brain hemorrhage.
The images, published by North Korean state media on Monday, show a seemingly animated Kim examining children’s footwear, gesturing toward officials and inspecting women’s coats at a garment and footwear exhibition.
The photos surfaced just hours after sensational claims circulated online that the 42-year-old leader had suffered a massive brain hemorrhage, fallen into a coma and died after being rushed to Beijing for emergency treatment.
North Korea’s official Korean Central News Agency reported that Kim toured the exhibition on Monday, although the photographs have not been independently authenticated and it remains unclear exactly when they were taken.
In one image, Kim bends forward to inspect a tiny pink shoe held by a young woman wearing a pale pink, double-breasted dress.
Another shows the North Korean strongman standing with his legs apart, his arms outstretched and his mouth open as he appears to speak emphatically with an official.
A third captures Kim reaching toward the sleeve of a rust-colored women’s coat displayed on a mannequin, while several aides trail behind him.
The apparent public appearance comes after Wanjun Xie, a US-based Chinese dissident associated with the China Democracy Party, posted a series of explosive allegations on X on Sunday.
Xie initially claimed that Kim had died and that China had dispatched 9,000 troops to Pyongyang amid fears of a succession crisis.
He subsequently alleged that a team of specialists from Beijing’s Peking Union Medical College Hospital had been sent to North Korea on Saturday to treat Kim following a severe cerebral hemorrhage.
According to Xie’s unsubstantiated account, the North Korean leader slipped into a coma before being transferred to Beijing, where doctors were unable to save him.
His body was then secretly returned to North Korea, Xie claimed.
NEW: Kim Jong Un on Monday "looked round the venue of the garment and footwear exhibition of the field of light industry," DPRK state media said. The photo-report came after rumors emerging on social media suggested he had died yesterday. https://t.co/rAZQMp2Uk6 pic.twitter.com/hmjRn06KX5
None of the allegations were accompanied by medical records, photographs, identifiable witnesses or other independently verifiable evidence.
The claims nevertheless gained traction across so cial media and were picked up by several international outlets, including The Sun, which characterized the story as unverified speculation.
The rumors also raised questions about whether Kim’s powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong , had taken control of the secretive regime.
The latest photographs, however, appear intended to dispel speculation about the North Korean leader’s fate, although Pyongyang has not explicitly addressed the death reports.
Kim’s health has long been a subject of international scrutiny.
On Sept. 30, South Korea’s National Intelligence Service told lawmakers that Kim weighed roughly 140 kilograms — about 309 pounds — and faced an elevated risk of cardiovascular disease because of his severe obesity.
Nevertheless, the spy agency said it had detected no significant signs of ill health , reportedly citing Kim’s ability to run up stairs during an inspection of a naval destroyer.
North Korean state media previously reported that Kim attended the inauguration of the National Defense Revolution Museum on Oct. 11, with an account of the ceremony published two days later.
That appearance preceded the alleged medical emergency and therefore could not refute claims that his condition had suddenly deteriorated.
Rumors circulate that Kim Jong-un has died, thwarting Kim Ju-ae's succession plans and potentially plunging North Korea into civil war. The Chinese Communist Party has reportedly dispatched 9,000 troops to Pyongyang to assist Kim Ju-ae in stabilizing her regime. In preparation…
It is said that On October 17, Peking Union Medical College Hospital dispatched a team of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular medical experts to North Korea to participate in the rescue of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, who was in critical condition.
It is rumored that recently,Kim Jong-un, General Secretary of the Workers' Party of Korea and Supreme Leader of North Korea, suffered a severe cerebral hemorrhage and fell into a coma. Although a team of medical experts from Peking Union Medical College Hospital was dispatched to…
The latest death scare also echoes a notorious false alarm in 2020, when Ji Seong-ho, a North Korean defector who became a South Korean lawmaker , claimed he was 99% certain Kim had died following cardiovascular surgery.
Kim subsequently appeared in public, and Ji apologized for spreading the erroneous claim.
That six-year-old prediction resurfaced during the latest frenzy, with some online accounts presenting it as fresh evidence that the North Korean leader had died.
The Post has sought comment from the governments of North Korea and China as well as from Peking Union Medical College Hospital.

articles.title_orig: From France to Albania, social unrest is setting Europe’s streets ablaze
articles.title_zh: From France to Albania, social unrest is setting Europe’s streets ablaze
articles.content_orig:
School conditions, unaffordable housing and the cost of living have brought demonstrators on to the streets in several countries
Europe live – latest updates
Young people have been taking to the streets across Europe, including in Spain, France and Portugal , to protest over their unhappiness at the state of schools and the wider cost of living crisis.
In France, high school pupils have clashed with police in often violent protests over long hours, missing teachers, dilapidated classrooms and an opaque university admissions system. Pupils routinely miss months of teaching due to unfilled staff absences.
Other demonstrators soon joined in, voicing their unhappiness about rising living costs, including over fuel prices after US bombing in effect caused the closure of the strait of Hormuz. The General Confederation of Labour, one of France’s largest unions, has backed the protests and called for lower prices, higher pensions and boosted wages.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron , is nearing the end of his time in the Élysée Palace after serving two terms.
Over the Pyrenees in Spain , activists took to the streets in September over housing prices.
The protests were triggered by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home after an investment fund hiked her rent by 230%. Maricarmen Abascal died a fortnight later after being admitted to hospital.
Protesters have called for rent freezes, halting the evictions of vulnerable people and the regulation of short-term and room rentals.
Similar pleas were made across the Iberian border in Portugal on Saturday, when hundreds gathered in central Lisbon . Portuguese housing prices more than doubled between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice as fast as the EU average, according to official data.
Squeezed household budgets were also at the centre of marches in Milan. Masked rioters seemingly later seized on the protests to throw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and setting fire to barricades made from bar tables. There were also clashes between police and protesters in Turin and Bologna.
Meanwhile, protests in Albania against the prime minister, Edi Rama, entered their seventh day on Monday. Demonstrators have said they are unhappy with perceived corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards.
The education protests in France began in late September, a week after the start of the school year. Protests soon also began springing up in Portugal and Belgium.
In France, demonstrations reached a high point on Saturday as about half a million people turned out to protest against the surging cost of living and join the students demanding better conditions at their schools. That day there were also marches in Belgium, Portugal and Italy.
In Albania, protests have been taking place since the summer, triggered by a luxury coastal development backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
In France, the government has said it will deploy 3,000 more substitute teachers to deal with shortages, and include students in decision-making for schools. It also scrapped plans to increase some university registration fees, which it had announced for next year’s budget.
Fuel protests in mid-September led to an announcement by the Élysée that the government would increase petrol subsidies for certain industries.
Spain’s Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, attempted to pass emergency housing legislation that included a ban on evictions until 2030 and the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.
The legislation’s defeat at the hands of rightwing and far-right parties in parliament led Sánchez to call a snap election for 29 November, as he told the public he needed a “broader progressive majority” to get new reforms through.
In recent days, the protests have been eclipsed by the violence that played out on the fringes. On Sunday night Macron said it was “unbearable to see our streets ransacked” while, hours later, France’s prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called for “very limited” and “localised” curfews.
Macron said a distinction must be drawn between what he described as genuine, peaceful demonstrators who were making demands over the cost of living and the education system, and others who “destroy, ransack and loot”.
His interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, appeared to signal the French government was not willing to concede further, as he blamed “far-left” protesters and “criminals who looted and ransacked” buildings across France. The country will go to the polls in April 2027.
Meanwhile, the protests continue. In Paris, about a dozen demonstrators blocked the entrance to the Louvre on Monday, leaving tourists milling outside the world’s most-visited museum.
In Spain, housing campaigners have vowed to keep up the pressure on politicians to address soaring costs, announcing plans for a general strike on 11 November.

articles.title_orig: Milan luxury shops close as Italy prepares to deploy troops in the city after days of protests
articles.title_zh: Milan luxury shops close as Italy prepares to deploy troops in the city after days of protests
articles.content_orig:
Demonstrations over poor public services and rising costs spiralled over the weekend, with shops looted and property vandalised
Why are people protesting across Europe?
Italy’s government will dispatch 500 army troops to “defend Milan” after two days ⁠of unrest that saw demonstrators ⁠clash with police, ​loot shops and vandalise property, deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini said on Monday.
The deployment is expected to be included in a package of security measures to be approved at ⁠a cabinet meeting expected on Tuesday, and comes as shops in central Milan closed early and boarded up their windows, fearing a fresh outbreak of violence in Italy’s financial capital.
“From words to action: 500 more ⁠troops to defend Milan,” Salvini, head of the co-ruling right-wing League party, wrote on social media.
Most stores in Milan’s Via ​Montenapoleone luxury shopping district, home to brands including Chanel, Tiffany ‌and Dior, had removed merchandise from ‌their windows as a precaution, while police patrolled the street and a handful of tourists looked on.
Several hundred hooded ‌protesters, many believed to be minors, set bins ablaze and looted shops in the city centre over the weekend after an initially peaceful demonstration on Saturday over poor public services and rising costs.
Among the stores ransacked were sports retailers Decathlon and Arc’teryx and mobile phone operator Vodafone, television footage showed. Clothing brands Levi’s and Under Armour, as well as Decathlon, covered their shop windows with cardboard and wooden panels.
Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, who ‌faces a national election next year, condemned the violence and chaired a meeting with ministers and security chiefs on Monday to discuss the situation.
“The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, ​including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors,” foreign minister Antonio Tajani, who also serves as deputy prime minister like Salvini, wrote on X.
As part of the planned crackdown, the Corriere della Sera newspaper said Meloni was considering extending preventive detention for minors and cracking down on youth gangs, while bringing forward some provisions contained in an existing security bill currently being examined by parliament.
Italian ⁠police said it had detained 271 young people during unrest in Milan on Sunday. Of ​those taken to police stations, 32 were ​arrested, including 23 minors and 13 ​foreign nationals, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.
The unrest followed ​clashes on Saturday in other northern cities ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, according to a police report released on Sunday.
The disturbances echoed unrest in neighbouring France , where hundreds of thousands of people angered by rising living costs and declining public services took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country’s most violent protests in years.

The run comes ahead of vital Q3 results that will follow this week, which are likely to set the tone for the trajectory of technology shares.
"Tech earnings are key this week. Fundamentals are unchanged, but given fragile price action, we turn neutral [on] risk assets and stay neutral duration," Ajay Rajadhyaksha, global chairman of research at Barclays, said in a note, according to CNBC.
Katie Stockton, founder of Fairlead Strategies, reportedly said in a note on Monday that the week will be crucial for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, which need to hold support, while noting that a hold is possible amid widespread, short-term oversold conditions.

AI-related power companies Bloom Energy (BE) and Valero Energy (VLO), along with big entertainment companies including Netflix Inc. (NFLX), will also announce their quarterly results.
Meanwhile, rising oil prices amid growing geopolitical uncertainty have put downward pressure on markets. Brent crude futures expiring in December were trading at $109.88 a barrel, up about 0.3%, while WTI crude futures expiring in November traded at $103.64 per barrel.
Economist Peter Schiff said in a post on X, "Oil rose another 2.5% today. It's almost $104. If you think gas prices are high now, just wait until after the midterms when Trump has to turn off the spigots from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to keep it from running dry. Oil could hit $150, sending gas prices to record highs."
Trump Media & Technology Group Corp. (DJT): Shares of the president's media company were in focus late Monday after the stock slipped 8%, its worst single-day drop since February, as President Donald Trump's approval rating hit a record low.
Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN): The company's stock surged nearly 5% at close on Monday and continued to climb higher overnight after Morgan Stanley raised its price target and named it a 'Top Pick.'
Cerebras Systems Inc. (CBRS): The AI hardware and supercomputing company was on the retail radar after shares slipped more than 5% on Monday, extending a broader selloff in the sector from last week.
CoreWeave Inc. (CRWV): Shares of the neocloud company fell more than 1% in overnight trading late Monday, putting it on track for a third week of declines amid a selloff in software names.
Among ETFs tracking benchmark indexes, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) all climbed overnight.
Meanwhile, U.S. long-dated Treasury yields continued above 5%. At the time of writing, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield was 5.138%, and the 30-year Treasury yield was 5.473%.
The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) was up 0.09% amid 'bullish' sentiment.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: OpenAI seeks to accelerate fundraising ahead of Anthropic IPO, sources say
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: OpenAI seeks to accelerate fundraising ahead of Anthropic IPO, sources say
articles.content_orig:
The spread is widening between AI leaders OpenAI and Anthropic as a sell-off in CoreWeave leads neocloud stocks lower.
OpenAI's valuation is down more than 4% the past 24 hours after briefly slipping under $1.5 trillion, according to perpetual futures pricing on decentralized exchange Hyperliquid. Meanwhile, Anthropic perps are up 2.4% over the same time period, recovering an overnight dip and indicating a valuation of just over $2 trillion.
Perpetuals are bets that never expire. They maintained by "deployers" on Hyperliquid's blockchain infrastructure that determine a funding rate for going long or short the futures based on a spot "oracle" price that uses third-party data like private funding rounds and secondary market transactions to estimate private-market prices.
Open interest, defined by Hyperliquid as the sum of long and short positions on a contract, is more than five times bigger in Anthropic than OpenAI — more than $41 million, compared to less than $7 million in OpenAI.
Right now the deployer behind these pre-IPO contracts – the developer building the exchange – is Entropy IO. TradeXYZ, the most prominent developer on the platform, typically does not list pre-IPO perps until S-1s are public, according to David Schamis, CEO of Hyperliquid Strategies , the publicly traded treasury company that invests in the HYPE token that powers the exchange.
"Liquidity will probably be deeper once TradeXYZ lists these companies," Schamis said in a call. "Generally these will trade at a premium to the IPO price but they do a good job predicting where it will be post-IPO."
The bigger price drop in OpenAI perps reflects the company's closer ties to GPU rent-a-center CoreWeave, whose shares touched a new one-year low Thursday, extending a decline over that period to 54%, as concerns mount over the company's debt-financing strategy.
In April, CoreWeave announced a deal with Anthropic to power the company's Claude products, but did not disclose the value of the deal. The company's relationship with OpenAI stretches back further, and as of September 2025 was worth at least $22 billion including a 5-year agreement to provide datacenters and technology.
While OpenAI perps are falling more than Anthropic the past 24 hours, the two are both down about 15% from highs last month, according to Hyperliquid pricing.

articles.title_orig: Christiane Amanpour is leaving CNN after 43 years
articles.title_zh: Christiane Amanpour is leaving CNN after 43 years
articles.content_orig:
CNN legend Christiane Amanpour, the network’s chief international anchor, said Monday that she will sign off from CNN next June.
“After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” Amanpour said in a statement.
Amanpour, 68, said she “looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.”
Amanpour, a household name worldwide for her heroism as a foreign correspondent, has hosted an eponymous nightly interview program on CNN International since 2009.
In January 2025, she scaled back to hosting a few days a week. In January 2027, she will shift the program to once a week, until it ends in May. She will continue reporting and traveling the world for CNN through June.
CNN chairman Mark Thompson shared Amanpour’s decision in a memo to colleagues Monday morning.
“Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months,” Thompson wrote. “Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.”
Thompson described her as “one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere” and said the network will take time to celebrate her “before she departs next year.”
“In the meantime, on behalf of the entire CNN leadership team, I want to thank Christiane for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship,” he wrote.
In her statement, Amanpour said she wanted to thank “all the amazingly talented people I’ve worked with throughout this incredible journey. Especially my beloved show teams and field crews.”
“From my very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between, it’s the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much,” she said, “as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor.”
Amanpour’s PBS iteration, “Amanpour & Company,” will end in December.
In her statement, Amanpour said she will continue her podcast, “ The Ex Files ,” with ex-husband Jamie Rubin, produced by Global.

articles.title_orig: Priest in Ecuador Dies After Crucifix Falls on Him During Livestreamed Mass
articles.title_zh: Priest in Ecuador Dies After Crucifix Falls on Him During Livestreamed Mass
articles.content_orig:
A priest has been killed by a falling crucifix at a church in Ecuador as he performed a mass that was being live streamed online.
Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari died on Saturday at the Perpetuo Socorro church in the city of Guayaquil, southern Ecuador, according to a statement from the city’s archdiocese, published on Facebook on Monday.
Video of the incident shows Sánchez leading the mass when a large wooden cross that was standing on the altar behind him falls over and hits him on the head.
Shouting can be heard from the congregation, and several people enter the frame and rush toward the priest.
On Sunday, the church held a eucharist in memory of Sánchez, led by Cardinal Luis Cabrera, archbishop of Guayaquil.
“We are grateful for all of the condolences from around the world, and especially for your prayers for the eternal rest of the soul of Patricio Sánchez,” the statement reads.
According to CNN affiliate Ecuavisa, the priest was preparing to lead a wedding ceremony when the tragedy occurred.
Police have not commented on the incident so far, Ecuavisa reported.
CNN has reached out to the Archdiocese of Guayaquil for comment.

articles.title_orig: Trump attacks ‘migrants and communists’ as he tries to exploit France unrest
articles.title_zh: Trump attacks ‘migrants and communists’ as he tries to exploit France unrest
articles.content_orig:
President at Kansas rally tries to turn protests into cautionary tale for US as Republicans face midterm losses
Explainer: why are people protesting across Europe?
As Republicans confront mounting political headwinds ahead of November’s midterm elections, Donald Trump is attempting to turn unrest in France into a cautionary tale for American voters, recasting the demonstrations that began as student protests against crumbling schools and the soaring cost of living as evidence of the dangers of immigration and the erosion of western civilization.
At a rally in Kansas on Monday evening, Trump described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists”.
“If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France ,” he said.
Nationwide protests in France on Saturday were called over rising fuel prices and falling purchasing power, and in several cities they erupted into looting and clashes with police that left a historic town hall torched and led to 1,800 arrests. On Monday, overnight curfews were issued for a number of French cities, including parts of Paris .
“This is what’s happening to France – they want to happen to our country. It’s never happening here,” Trump declared, drawing loud cheers from the thousands-strong crowd in ruby-red Kansas where the Republican senator, Roger Marshall, is facing a surprisingly tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton.
Earlier in the day, Trump repeated his baseless claim that migrants had “taken over” France, writing on Truth Social that the country’s leaders must “CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!”
The rhetoric echoes France’s far-right National Rally , whose president, Jordan Bardella, described the violence as a convergence of ultra-left extremism and delinquent populations from the suburbs. Trump and Vance have both publicly backed Marine Le Pen, and the unrest has added pressure on Emmanuel Macron six months before an April election to choose his successor.
As Trump set off for the Kansas rally on Monday, the US president told reporters at the White House that he had warned Macron he was “making a big mistake”.
“The whole world was coming in, and as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn’t the deal,” he said, adding: “We closed our borders. He didn’t.”
Before Trump arrived on stage in Park City, Kansas, giant TV screens played about 10 minutes’ of Fox News coverage of the unrest that has gripped Paris and other cities, which included commentary blaming the trouble on the French government’s immigration policies.
The demonstrations in France began weeks ago, when high school students began marching for teacher shortages, crumbling classrooms and an opaque university admissions system. The CGT, one of France’s largest unions, has backed the movement and called for lower prices, higher pensions and better wages. The anger has since widened to fuel prices, which have climbed since US strikes effectively shut the strait of Hormuz, and other economic grievances.
As the midterms loom, the unrest in France offers Trump a familiar politcal opportunity: the chance to transform a crisis on the other side of the Atlantic into an argument in favor of the hard-line immigration policies that helped propel Trump’s return to the White House.
“If you import the third world, you become the third world,” the official White House X account posted earlier in the day..
JD Vance and array of Republican politicians have lined up to make a similar argument.
Sharing a video that showed the historic city hall in Limoges alight, vice-president JD Vance argued that the rioting was the result of what he called a liberal failure. “Western liberals imported the third world into France,” he wrote on X, adding that the country had “ignored fundamental questions about assimilation and compatibility”.
House Speaker Mike Johnson posted: “France is descending into chaos because they wanted OPEN BORDERS — just like the socialist Democrats in America. What we are witnessing is a chilling warning for all Americans of what happens if the radical Marxist insurgent left gets their way.” Senator Eric Schmitt added: “The anti-civilization Left is devouring France. It will devour America if we let it.”
Not all protests have drawn the same attention from Washington, as young people have taken to the streets across Europe , in Spain, Portugal and Italy, over underfunded schools, housing costs and a wider squeeze on living standards.
Neither has the president commented on protests in Albania , where demonstrators have targeted both the government and a luxury tourism development backed by an investment firm founded by Trump’s close familyson-in-law, Jared Kushner.
But Republicans are eager to keep the attention on France, as they warn of threats to the national identity and seek to rally support for Trump’s Make America Great Again movement.
The vice president said he hoped Americans were paying attention as they cast their ballots.
“This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country,” Vance concluded.

articles.title_orig: Gangs in Haiti target foreign troops in the biggest attack since a new force began operations
articles.title_zh: Gangs in Haiti target foreign troops in the biggest attack since a new force began operations
articles.content_orig:
More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces
At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.
There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.
Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.
Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.
The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.
The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.
The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.
“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”
A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”
They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”
Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.
The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month .
Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.
A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.
The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.
Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.
